title: You Are Not Perceiving the World, You Are Predicting It: The Brain Fabricates the Reality You See
dek: Perception is not passively receiving external signals, but a prediction made by the brain based on the body's internal state; the world and self you experience are controlled hallucinations constrained by sensations, all ultimately serving to sustain life.
why: A TED-style talk that uses three experiments—a checkerboard, noise, and a rubber hand—to explain predictive processing, and clearly answers whether AI can have perception. Suitable for beginners; not many cutting-edge details.
who: Engineers working on AI consciousness or brain-computer interfaces, founders trying to judge whether AI will have self-awareness, and tech investors who need to distinguish intelligence from feeling.
skip: Listeners familiar with predictive processing can skip the checkerboard and noise demonstrations from 5:10 to 10:20 and go straight to the self section.

points.h: General anesthesia is not sleep; it is total nonexistence
points.body: The speaker disappeared completely during his third surgery under general anesthesia: as the anesthetic filled his brain, he felt dissociation, fragmentation, and cold, then woke up, but with no sense of continuous time in between. Waking from deep sleep, you know how long has passed, but waking from general anesthesia could be 5 minutes, 5 hours, 5 years, or even 50 years—he simply was not there. This total disappearance is worth taking seriously because it turns "how consciousness happens" into one of the biggest remaining puzzles in science and philosophy: how do billions of neurons produce the present you?

points.h: You see what your brain expects to see
points.body: The brain is locked inside the skull, with no light or sound, and all it gets are streams of electrical impulses only indirectly related to external objects. Perception is therefore not reading in the world but informed guessing: the brain combines sensory signals with prior expectations about "what the world is probably like" to guess the most likely cause. In the checkerboard shadow illusion, squares A and B are exactly the same gray, but because the visual cortex knows a priori that "shadows darken surfaces," B is seen as brighter; the same meaningless noise suddenly becomes intelligible words after hearing the original sentence. The sensory input does not change; only the brain's guess about the cause changes.

points.h: The world is generated from the inside out
points.body: Since perception is active guessing, the brain uses not only sensory signals from the outside but equally, or even more importantly, predictions sent inward. The Sussex team's demonstration processes campus videos with an algorithm similar to Deep Dream, simulating what the brain sees when predictions are too strong: dogs everywhere, the image becoming like a hallucinogenic state or the visual experience of psychosis. The conclusion is steep: if hallucination is uncontrolled perception, then normal perception right now is also a hallucination, but a controlled one—the brain's predictions are constrained by sensory signals from the world.

points.h: The self is also a hallucination generated by the brain
points.body: The experience of being "you" is also generated by the brain, and it is not a single thing: there is the experience of "having a body" and "existing as a body," the experience of perceiving the world from a first-person perspective, the experience of intending to act and being the cause of external events, and the experience of a "continuous unique personality over time" maintained by memory and social interaction. Psychiatry and neurology already know these dimensions can be dissociated from each other. The so-called unified and continuous self is actually a fragile brain construction, just as much in need of explanation as vision.

points.h: The brain can claim a fake hand as its own
points.body: The rubber hand illusion can be done at home: your real hand is hidden, a fake hand is placed in front of you, and two brushes stroke both the real and fake hands simultaneously while you stare at the fake hand. After a while, the fake hand vaguely becomes part of your body. The reason is that the visual and tactile inputs are consistent, the shape resembles a hand, and the position is roughly where a hand should be—these pieces of evidence are enough for the brain to guess "this is my hand." Threatening the fake hand directly with a hammer reveals that the subject has incorporated it into their body. Peter Lush at Sussex found that the strength of this illusion is highly correlated with hypnotic suggestibility: the experimental setup itself is suggesting "the fake hand belongs to you," so people who are easily suggestible naturally have that experience more readily.

points.h: Heartbeat synchronization makes the fake hand feel more like your own
points.body: Besides perceiving the body as an external object, the brain also perceives the body from within, known as interoception: heartbeat, blood pressure, and visceral states constantly tell the brain how things are inside. This perception is often overlooked, but it is precisely what keeps the body alive. In the VR version of the rubber hand experiment at the Sussex lab, a virtual hand flashes red and black either in sync or out of sync with the heartbeat; when in sync, subjects are significantly more likely to feel it is part of their body. Body ownership is thus shown to be deeply rooted in the perception of the internal body.

points.h: Internal perception is not for knowing, but for staying alive
points.body: The experience from inside the body is completely different from seeing the external world: you do not perceive "the kidney is here, the liver is there, the spleen is somewhere"—internal organs barely enter consciousness unless they malfunction. This is because the brain's purpose for internal perception is not to determine what is there, but to control and regulate, keeping physiological variables like blood pressure and heart rate within a narrow range suitable for survival. When predictions are used to identify external objects, we experience "seeing something"; when predictions are used to regulate the body, we experience how well control is going. So the most basic self-experience is directly rooted in the mechanisms that keep the organism alive.

points.h: Smarter computers do not mean conscious ones
points.body: Finally, three consequences are given. First, since we can misperceive the world, we can also misperceive ourselves when predictions go wrong; this gives psychiatry and neurology the opportunity to target mechanisms rather than just treating symptoms of depression and schizophrenia. Second, "I am me" cannot be reduced to or uploaded as software running on a robot, no matter how smart or complex—we are flesh-and-blood animals, and conscious experience is shaped at every level by biological mechanisms that sustain life. Third, each of us has our own inner universe, and human consciousness is just a small region in a vast space of possible consciousness. So just making computers smarter will not make them sentient.

terms.def: The brain actively generates experience while being constrained by sensory signals; normal perception is a controlled hallucination.
The brain's perception of internal states such as heartbeat and blood pressure, aimed not at recognition but at regulation and survival.
Perception is the brain's guess about the causes of the world, combining sensory signals with prior expectations.

quotes.text: Consciousness and intelligence are very different things. You don't have to be smart to suffer, but you probably do have to be alive.
We don't just passively perceive our worlds. We actively generate them.
In fact, we're all hallucinating all the time, including right now. It's just that when we agree about our hallucinations, that's what we call reality.
Perception of the internal state of the body isn't about figuring out what's there. It's about control and regulation.
Just making computers smarter is not going to make them sentient.
